name: Johor Sultanate
capital: Johor Lama / Riau (capital moved several times)

knownFor.label: Riverine capitals
knownFor.note: Capitals moved along the Johor river and to the Riau islands.

knownFor.label: Gambier & pepper plantations
knownFor.note: Chinese-run plantations under the kangchu system.

knownFor.label: Sejarah Melayu (Malay Annals)
knownFor.note: The classic history of the Melaka–Johor royal line, edited in Johor.

location.value: The southern Malay Peninsula and the Riau-Lingga islands. At its height it included modern Johor, Pahang, Terengganu, Singapore, the Riau islands and parts of east Sumatra (Siak, Kampar).

terrain.value: River estuaries (the Johor River) and island harbours (Riau, Lingga) on the southern Strait of Malacca and the Singapore Strait.

climate.value: Equatorial and monsoonal, setting the sailing seasons of the straits trade.
climate.source: Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

resources.value: Tin, pepper, gambier, and forest and sea products. Riau became a spice entrepôt with Bugis traders.

disasters.value: No major natural disasters are recorded. The main destruction was from enemy raids on its capitals.

population.value: No population figure is available in the sources checked.

urbanisation.value: Small river and island capitals that moved frequently (Johor Lama, Batu Sawar, Kota Tinggi, Riau). Riau became a busy port in the 17th–18th centuries.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Bugis and Minangkabau settlers and warriors became powerful in the late 17th–18th centuries. The Orang Laut (sea peoples) were key subjects.

economicBase.value: Entrepôt trade and port duties (which were kept low), plus tin and pepper.

tradeRoutes.value: Traders from Cambodia, Siam, Vietnam, China and across the Malay Archipelago. Chinese cloth and opium were exchanged for tin, pepper, gambier and forest products.

moneyAndTax.value: Tin ingots and local gold and silver coins. Low port duties attracted traders.

inequality.value: A sultan and noble officials (Bendahara, Temenggong, Orang Kaya) controlled trade, above commoners and dependants.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy, with the sultan advised by Orang Kaya nobles, the Bendahara (chief minister) and the Temenggong.

keyRulers.value: Alauddin Riayat Shah II (1528–1564, founder, son of Melaka’s last sultan). Abdul Jalil Shah III (1623–1677). Mahmud Shah II (assassinated 1699). Abdul Jalil IV (the former Bendahara). Abdul Rahman Muazzam Shah (1811–1819).

succession.value: Descended from the Melaka royal line until 1699, when Sultan Mahmud II was killed with no heir and the Bendahara family took the throne.

institutions.value: The Melaka-style offices of Bendahara and Temenggong, and Islamic law. Riau became a centre of Islamic learning.

stability.value: Often unstable: capitals were sacked by Aceh, Portugal and Jambi, and Raja Kecil’s rebellion (1718) was followed by Bugis dominance.

eliteConflict.value: The assassination of Mahmud II (1699) after he ordered a noble’s pregnant wife killed. Later rivalry between Malay nobles and Bugis chiefs.

armyAndTech.value: Naval forces drawn from the Orang Laut, later Bugis fighters. Fleet and army sizes are not stated.

majorWars.value: Long “triangular war” with Portugal and Aceh (1528–1641). Helped the Dutch capture Portuguese Malacca (14 January 1641). The Johor–Jambi war (1666–1679), in which Batu Sawar was sacked in 1673.

territoryChange.value: Regained power after 1641. Lost Siak and other Sumatran territories in the 18th century. Split by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824.

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with the Dutch VOC (treaties of 1606, the 1641 Malacca siege). Rivals were Portuguese Malacca, Aceh and Jambi.

inventions.value: Malay shipbuilding and navigation. No specific inventions are documented.

scienceEducation.value: Riau became a centre of Islamic studies, with scholars from India and Arabia. Later the Riau court produced Raja Ali Haji’s Malay grammar and literature (19th century).
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Johor Sultanate (checked 5 Nov 2026); Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

openness.value: Open to foreign traders and alliances (Dutch, Bugis, Chinese merchants).

languageWriting.value: Classical Malay in Jawi script. The Riau-Johor dialect became the basis of standard Malay and Indonesian.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Johor Sultanate (checked 5 Nov 2026); Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

artsArchitecture.value: Malay court literature continued the Melaka tradition (the Sejarah Melayu was reworked under Johor patronage in 1612).
artsArchitecture.source: Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

socialStructure.value: Sultan, nobles, Orang Laut followers, commoners, and debt-bondsmen.
socialStructure.source: Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

sharedIdentity.value: Claimed the legacy of Melaka as its successor. A key source of Malay royal identity.

neighbours.value: Aceh, Portuguese (later Dutch) Malacca, Jambi, Siak, Pahang, Patani and Siam.

ideasReligions.value: A hub of Islamic learning and Malay literature in the Riau islands.

colonisation.value: Colonised in effect. The 1824 Anglo-Dutch Treaty split the realm, with the mainland under British influence and Riau under the Dutch. Raffles’ 1819 Singapore agreement had already used a rival claimant.

riseSignals.value: Founded by Melaka’s royal heir after 1511. Recovered once Aceh weakened (1629) and the Dutch took Malacca (1641). Riau’s trade boom followed.

peakPeriod.value: The late 17th-century trade boom at Riau, when territory stretched across both sides of the strait.

declineSignals.value: The destructive Jambi war (1666–79), the 1699 regicide ending the Melaka line, Raja Kecil’s 1718 rebellion, and dependence on Bugis power.

outcome.value: Partitioned by the 1824 Anglo-Dutch Treaty into a British-influenced mainland and the Dutch-controlled Riau-Lingga Sultanate. A Johor sultanate continues today as a state of Malaysia.

sources.value: Malay texts (Sejarah Melayu, Tuhfat al-Nafis), Portuguese, Dutch and British records. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Andaya & Andaya (2017).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. The end date depends on definition (1819, 1824, 1877, or ongoing as the modern state). There are no population figures. Second source: Wikidata continues the sultanate to 1946; this app’s entry ends with the 1824 split of Johor-Riau.
